---
title: "Six-Sided Die"
description: "Symmetry helps before discreteness disappears"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("../R/populations.R")
source("../R/diagnostics.R")
source("../R/simulation.R")
source("../R/plots.R")
library(ggplot2)
population <- get_population("die")
diagnostics <- read.csv("../results/diagnostics.csv")
page_results <- diagnostics[diagnostics$population == "die", ]
bands <- read.csv("../results/calibration_bands.csv")
selected_n <- c(1, 10, 30)
simulation <- simulate_population(population, selected_n, B = 10000L, seed = 631L, keep_means = TRUE)
```

## 1. Question and prediction

A die is bounded and symmetric, so I expected its sample mean to become bell-shaped relatively quickly. The main obstacle should be visible spacing between possible means, not skewness.

## 2. Parent population

```{r}
#| label: fig-die-parent
#| fig-cap: "Each die face has probability 1/6. The parent is perfectly symmetric but discrete, which separates the effects of asymmetry and lattice spacing."
#| fig-alt: "Six equal bars for die outcomes one through six."
plot_parent_population(population)
```

## 3. Theory before simulation

For one fair die, $E(X)=3.5$ and $Var(X)=35/12$. Independence, identical distribution, and finite variance hold, so

$$
E(\bar X_n)=3.5, \qquad SE(\bar X_n)=\sqrt{\frac{35}{12n}}.
$$

The ordinary CLT applies.

## 4. Simulation design

The grid is dense near the expected transition: 1 through 6, then 8, 10, 12, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 75, and 100. Each point uses 10,000 means and seed 631.

## 5. Numerical evidence

```{r}
#| label: tbl-die-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "Die diagnostics around the transition. Center and SE agree early; excess kurtosis settles before Q-Q RMSE because a discrete lattice remains visible."
shown <- page_results[page_results$n %in% c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50), c("n", "mean_error", "relative_se_error", "skewness", "excess_kurtosis", "qq_rmse")]
names(shown) <- c("n", "Center error", "Relative SE error", "Skewness", "Excess kurtosis", "Q-Q RMSE")
knitr::kable(shown, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

At $n=30$, the simulated center is `r sprintf("%.4f", page_results$simulated_mean[page_results$n == 30])` and the empirical SE is `r sprintf("%.4f", page_results$simulated_se[page_results$n == 30])`, close to the theoretical `r sprintf("%.4f", page_results$theoretical_se[page_results$n == 30])`.

## 6. Shape across sample sizes

```{r}
#| label: fig-die-sampling
#| fig-cap: "The die mean progresses from six isolated outcomes at n = 1 to a bell-shaped lattice at n = 10 and a much finer bell at n = 30. Dark curves show theoretical Normal references; the last shape is useful despite residual spacing."
#| fig-alt: "Three histograms showing six spikes, then increasingly fine symmetric bell shapes."
plot_sampling_distributions(simulation$means, population, selected_n)
```

## 7. Q-Q evidence

```{r}
#| label: fig-die-qq
#| fig-cap: "Q-Q points straighten as n grows, but stair steps remain at n = 30 because sample means occupy a lattice. This explains why Q-Q RMSE stays above the continuous Normal calibration."
#| fig-alt: "Three Q-Q panels becoming straighter while retaining small steps."
plot_qq_comparison(simulation$means, population, selected_n)
```

## 8. Diagnostic trajectory

```{r}
#| label: fig-die-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "Absolute skewness, excess kurtosis, and Q-Q RMSE over n. The red lines are Normal-calibrated guidance bands; the persistent Q-Q disagreement is a discreteness effect rather than asymmetry."
#| fig-alt: "Three line charts showing shape diagnostics generally declining with sample size."
plot_diagnostic_trajectory(page_results, population, bands)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-die-se
#| fig-cap: "Empirical and theoretical standard errors nearly overlap across n. Precision follows theory before the lattice becomes visually close to Normal."
#| fig-alt: "Two nearly overlapping standard-error curves declining as die sample size increases."
plot_se_comparison(page_results, population)
```

## 9. Decision and disagreement

**Decision: $n=30$.** The histogram is symmetric and sufficiently smooth for a practical Normal approximation, the center and SE are accurate, and the conclusion remains credible at $n=40$ and $n=50$. Q-Q RMSE still exceeds the stringent Normal-noise band. I retain that disagreement because it correctly detects lattice spacing, but it does not make the global approximation misleading.

## 10. Limitation and surprise

The selected threshold depends on the intended use. A continuity-sensitive tail calculation may need a larger $n$ than a central probability approximation. The notable surprise is that symmetry solves the skewness problem immediately, while discreteness leaves a longer numerical fingerprint.
